## Data-grounded hypothesis (final answer)

**Prevalence definition used:** per-habitat share of non-native species records attributable to the Gardening pathway, i.e., Σn.gard / Σn.total aggregated over plots within each habitat (plot-level dataset, 632 plots in Barcelona province); species-level occupancy is used as a supporting metric, not the main claim.

**Hypothesis:** The prevalence of non-native plants introduced via gardening varies strongly across habitat types: it is highest in semi-natural, woody and moist habitats — dominating broad-leaved forests (100% of the 4 non-native records), coniferous forests (87.5%, 7/8), wetlands (55.8%) and coastal habitats (53.5%) — and lowest in heavily modified or sparsely vegetated habitats dominated by unintentional introductions, i.e., croplands (18.5%), urban areas (29.8%), meadows (30.8%) and rock outcrops (0%). Overall, Gardening accounts for 35.1% of non-native species records (169 of 481). A binomial GLM on the 191 plots with ≥1 non-native species (successes = n.gard, failures = n.total − n.gard) confirms the gardening share of the non-native flora differs significantly among habitats (LR χ² = 50.62, df = 9, p = 8.2×10⁻⁸), and this habitat effect persists after adjusting for plot-level elevation, 2009 urban/cropland cover (500 m buffer) and distances to roads and streams (LR χ² = 45.79, df = 9, p = 6.6×10⁻⁷); if anything, higher surrounding urban cover lowers the gardening share (coefficient −1.25, p = 0.028), so the variation is not simply an urbanization artifact. Supporting contingency tests corroborate the enrichment of gardening species in forests/wetlands/coastal habitats (Fisher p = 0.003–0.015) and their depletion in croplands (p < 0.001); a habitat × pathway chi-square is highly significant (χ² = 75.2, df = 18, p = 5.8×10⁻⁹).

**Important caveat and mechanism:** gardening-introduced species are individually less prevalent at the species level — they occupy fewer invaded plots (median 2 vs 3; mean 3.9 vs 9.6; Mann–Whitney p = 0.058), smaller 10-km areas of occupancy (p = 0.035) and narrower invaded niche breadth (0.38 vs 0.84; p = 0.015) than unintentional species — so the high habitat-level gardening shares in forests/wetlands/coastal habitats reflect a strong concentration of gardening species in those habitat types rather than broad spatial spread of individual species. The two highest shares (broad-leaved and coniferous forests) rest on only 4 and 8 non-native records (3 and 5 invaded plots), with model CIs of 0–1 and 0.46–0.98 respectively, so those extreme values are not reliable; the most robust contrasts are the elevated shares in wetlands (CI 0.42–0.69) and coastal habitats (CI 0.39–0.68) versus the depressed share in croplands (CI 0.12–0.27). The pattern is also consistent with the regional temporal context in which Gardening is the fastest-growing pathway, rising from 16.8% of introductions before 1500 to 75.2% in 1985–2019 (n = 397 in the latest period).

payload.hypothesis: The prevalence of non-native plants introduced via gardening varies strongly by habitat type: it dominates semi-natural woody and moist habitats (broad-leaved forests 100% of 4 records, coniferous forests 87.5% of 8, wetlands 55.8%, coastal 53.5%) and is lowest in modified/intensively used habitats where unintentional introductions dominate (croplands 18.5%, urban 29.8%, meadows 30.8%, rock outcrops 0%), with an overall 35.1% gardening share of non-native species records. The habitat effect is statistically strong (binomial GLM LRT chi2=50.62, df=9, p=8.2e-08) and persists after adjusting for elevation, urban/cropland cover and distances to roads/streams (chi2=45.79, df=9, p=6.6e-07). Gardening species are individually less plot-prevalent than unintentional species (median 2 vs 3 invaded plots, p=0.058; narrower invaded niche breadth 0.38 vs 0.84, p=0.015), so the high habitat-level shares reflect concentration of gardening species in forests/wetlands/coastal habitats rather than broad spread. The two highest forest shares rest on very few records (4 and 8) and are imprecise (CI 0-1 and 0.46-0.98); the most robust contrasts are elevated wetland/coastal shares vs depressed cropland share. Gardening is contextually the fastest-growing pathway regionally (16.8% to 75.2% of introductions over time periods).
payload.workflow: 1) Aggregated per-habitat gardening share (sum n.gard / sum n.total over 632 plot rows); 2) binomial GLM successes=n.gard, failures=n.total-n.gard among the 191 plots with n.total>0, with LRT for the habitat term and per-habitat predicted shares with 95% CI; Poisson offset=log(n.total) as robustness; 3) confounder check adding urban/cropland % (2009, 500m), elevation, distance.road, distance.stream, with LRTs for habitat-after-covariates and covariates-on-top-of-habitat; 4) habitat x pathway chi-square plus per-habitat Fisher tests; 5) species-level Mann-Whitney/Wilcoxon tests (Gardening vs Unintentional) on number.of.invaded.plots, area.of.occupancy.10km, habitat.range, invaded.niche.breadth with rank-biserial effect sizes, plus sensitivity dropping duplicated (two-pathway) rows and Kruskal-Wallis across 3 pathways; 6) temporal gardening-share trend as context only.
